title: The Cat of the Windows
summary: On a cold, dark street sits a small gray stray cat, with no home and no one at all. Then, in one window, a candle is lit, and every night of Hanukkah there's another window and another light, until the whole street and the whole city glow. "Meow! Window after window, light after light!" But someone behind the very first window has been watching him all along... A warm rhyming story about Hanukkah candles placed in the window so everyone passing outside can see the light.
pages:
On a cold, dark street, on a winter night, by the trash bin there,
sat a small gray cat with a torn ear, sighing into the air.
"Meow. I'm cold. And it's dark. And I have no home, and no one at all."
And then, in one window up high, hop! a little light was lit. Alone. So small.

One candle and the shamash stood in the window, looking out at the street,
as if telling everyone passing by, "Look! Look! Isn't it sweet!"
The cat sat below and gazed and gazed, and it felt like... warm.
Even though it was cold. Even though it was dark. Even with no one in the world, through the storm.

On the second night, two windows! On the third night, three!
A clay menorah, a menorah made of bottle caps, a shiny new silver one to see.
Meow! Window after window, light after light!

And in every window, a little story: here they spin a dreidel, here they sing,
here Grandpa in a hat plays the violin, here they eat sufganiyot and get sticky with everything.
The cat went from window to window, like a show, with no ticket and no line in sight,
because Hanukkah candles go in the window, so everyone passing outside can see the light.

On the fourth night and the fifth, the whole building lit up, floor after floor!
And the cat climbed: up a drainpipe, a balcony, a flowerpot, wet laundry, and more!
Meow! Window after window, light after light!

On the sixth night and the seventh, he sat on the roof and looked: windows, windows, thousands of them, near and far!
And little lights twinkled below, like an upside-down sky, with every light a star.
Meow! Window after window, light after light!

And on the eighth night, he went back to the very first window. And waited.
And there: eight candles and the shamash, and behind them... a girl! She waved to him. Like this. Elated.

Every night she had seen him sitting outside, watching, small and gray.
"Ima! Abba!" she called. "My cat! He came again! He came to see the light today!"

The door opened, creak! and there stood the girl, with a saucer of milk and a blanket in hand.
"Come," she whispered, "come, cat. There's room here. And there's Hanukkah, just as we planned."
The cat looked... and looked... and then came in, slowly, step after step,
and Abba, in his kippah, shut the door: click. And the cold stayed outside. Alone. Left.

And now, on the windowsill, beside eight candles and the shamash, sits a gray cat, snug and bright,
looking out at the street, at whoever passes in the cold of the night.
And a little boy outside, in a kippah and mittens, stops and points and laughs with delight:
Meow! Window after window, light after light!
